hints: Recall the three characteristic colours of silver halide precipitates for chloride, bromide and iodide.
walkthrough:
Link the observation to the halide test**
Warming with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$ hydrolyses the halogenoalkane to release $\text{X}^{-}\text{(aq)}$. Adding $\text{AgNO}_{3}\text{(aq)}$ then gives $\text{AgX(s)}$. A cream precipitate is the classic colour for silver bromide, white is chloride and yellow is iodide.

hints: Focus only on the ions that combine to make the solid, leaving out spectator ions like $\text{Na}^{+}$ and $\text{NO}_{3}^{-}$.
walkthrough:
Build the precipitation equation**
The free bromide ion from hydrolysis meets silver ion to form the insoluble solid. So write $\text{Ag}^{+}$ plus $\text{Br}^{-}$ giving $\text{AgBr}$. Both ions are in aqueous solution and the product is a solid, so add $\text{(aq)}$ to reactants and $\text{(s)}$ to the product: $$\text{Ag}^{+}\text{(aq)} + \text{Br}^{-}\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{AgBr(s)}$$

hints: Think about which reagent is used to test the solubility of silver halide precipitates after they have formed.
Recall how $\text{AgCl}$, $\text{AgBr}$ and $\text{AgI}$ differ in dilute versus concentrated aqueous ammonia.
walkthrough:
Choose the confirmatory reagent**
Silver halides look similar, so you test solubility in ammonia. Add aqueous ammonia to the cream precipitate.

Predict the behaviour of AgBr**
Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia, silver bromide needs concentrated ammonia to dissolve, and silver iodide stays insoluble even in concentrated ammonia. So for bromide you see partial or no dissolving in dilute $\text{NH}_{3}\text{(aq)}$ but complete dissolving in concentrated $\text{NH}_{3}\text{(aq)}$, which confirms $\text{Br}^{-}$.

Final answer: test: add (aqueous) ammonia
Expected result: with dilute ammonia little or no precipitate dissolves, with concentrated ammonia precipitate dissolves

hints: Remember that $S_{N}2$ is favoured by the least hindered carbon, so consider where the $\text{Br}$ must be on a straight five carbon chain.
walkthrough:
Pick the isomer that favours S_N2**
Q is straight chain $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{Br}$. $S_{N}2$ needs easy attack by $\text{OH}^{-}$ at the $\text{C-Br}$ carbon. That is easiest at a terminal primary carbon with least crowding. So place $\text{Br}$ on carbon 1: $$\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{Br}$$ This is 1-bromopentane.

hints: Think about what intermediate an $S_{N}1$ pathway would have to form first by loss of $\text{Br}^{-}$.
Consider how many alkyl groups can donate electron density to that positive carbon in a primary halogenoalkane.
walkthrough:
Picture the S_N1 intermediate**
In $S_{N}1$, the $\text{C-Br}$ bond breaks first to give a carbocation. From 1-bromopentane you would get $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}^{+}$, a primary carbocation.

Explain why it is unstable**
Alkyl groups stabilise a carbocation by pushing electron density toward $\text{C}^{+}$ through the positive inductive effect, spreading the charge. Here there is only one alkyl group attached to $\text{C}^{+}$, so stabilisation is weak and the charge stays concentrated. That high energy intermediate makes $S_{N}1$ unfavourable, so the one step $S_{N}2$ attack is preferred.

Final answer: The $S_{N}1$ route would form a primary carbocation which is not very stable.
Only one alkyl group can exert a positive inductive effect, so the positive charge remains localised on $\text{C}^{+}$.

hints: Note the conditions are NaOH in ethanol heated under reflux and the product is an alkene, not an alcohol.
walkthrough:
Recognise elimination from reagents and product**
Aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ gives substitution to an alcohol, but ethanolic $\text{NaOH}$ with heat removes $\text{HCl}$ from the halogenoalkane to form a $\text{C=C}$ double bond. Forming methylpropene from $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Cl}$ is therefore elimination.

hints: Write the reactants as $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Cl}$ plus $\text{NaOH}$ and remember elimination of a chloroalkane also produces $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Balance the elimination equation**
Remove $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cl}$ from the chloroalkane to give the alkene $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}$. The $\text{H}$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{Na}$ and $\text{O}$ combine as $\text{NaCl}$ plus $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$. Check atoms balance: $$\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8} + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_{2}\text{O}$$

hints: Draw methylpropene as a three carbon chain with a double bond and a methyl branch on the second carbon, then convert to skeletal lines.
walkthrough:
Sketch methylpropene in skeletal form**
Methylpropene is $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$, also called 2-methylpropene. In skeletal notation each vertex is a carbon and hydrogens are hidden. Draw a $\text{C=C}$ double line, with two short single lines branching from the left carbon for the two $\text{CH}_{3}$ groups and no branch on the right $\text{=CH}_{2}$ carbon.
Final answer: Skeletal formula of $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ only: a double line for $\text{C=C}$ with a single line branch for the second methyl group

hints: Work backwards by adding $\text{H}$ and $\text{Cl}$ across the $\text{C=C}$ of $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ in different positions.
Look for the two different $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{9}\text{Cl}$ skeletons that can lose $\text{HCl}$ to give only that branched alkene.
walkthrough:
Find the tertiary chloride**
Adding $\text{Cl}$ to the central carbon of $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$ gives $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{3}\text{CCl}$. That is 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, a tertiary halogenoalkane. It eliminates readily to give methylpropene.

Find the primary chloride with the same skeleton**
Adding $\text{Cl}$ to the terminal $\text{CH}_{2}$ carbon gives $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{CHCH}_{2}\text{Cl}$. That is 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, a primary halogenoalkane. Loss of $\text{H}$ from the central carbon also gives only $\text{(CH}_{3}\text{)}_{2}\text{C=CH}_{2}$. These are the two isomers P and R in either order.
